clue.text: Monarch working to get in style over a long time

indicators.note: getting in means passing inside something, so one pair of words goes within the other

blocks.note: R, for Rex or Regina, is the abbreviation for a monarch
a machine that is working is on
chic means stylishness

explanation.surface: A king is busy trying to acquire some elegance, and it takes him ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over a long time' reads like the end of the wordplay, but it is the whole definition: chronic as in lasting.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronic condition persists for a long period, so the adjective describes something lasting over a long time.

clue.text: Dismiss consequence of 'exeunt omnes'?

blocks.note: first meaning: discard or reject
second meaning, read as two words: the actors have all left the stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Exeunt omnes' is the stage direction 'all leave', so afterwards the players of the play are off the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast off means discard; read as cast plus off, it describes the actors having gone.

clue.text: Prompt to secure a rest

indicators.note: securing something means holding it firmly within, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a reminder prompts the memory
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to get some sleep booked in.
explanation.definitionFit: The remainder is what is left over, the rest of something.

clue.text: Endless sex – turned on, right? – in corner

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: nooky is British slang for sex
surface aside that also confirms the letters a second way, explained below

explanation.surface: A cheeky aside about sex in a corner, checking someone is aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: The aside gives the same letters a second way: 'turned on' is ON read backwards, NO, and 'right' is OK, so NO + OK confirms the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a small recess or corner of a room.

clue.text: Car crashed in the clover

indicators.note: something crashed is wrecked and scattered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A car has come off the road and ended up in a field of clover.
explanation.definitionFit: Chevrolet is an American car brand, part of General Motors, so it is a type of car.

clue.text: Competition set to take a different direction in Durham town

indicators.note: going the other way means the word is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: Consett is a former steel town in County Durham
names the three letters already inside the town's name that are to be turned round

explanation.surface: A competition in a County Durham town is due to change course.
explanation.walkthrough: CONSETT, a town in County Durham in north-east England, already contains SET; turn that SET round in place and you get CONTEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest is a competition between rivals, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Pick up what hasn't been dropped?

blocks.note: first meaning: to grab or hear something
second meaning: in cricket, a ball held cleanly by a fielder

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a fielder who holds the ball without dropping it takes one of these, getting the batter out.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch is to seize something, and a held ball in cricket or baseball is also called by this noun.

clue.text: Trivial information turned up, readable but with one misprint

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word runs upwards, from bottom to top
a misprint is one wrong letter, so one letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
legible writing can be read

explanation.surface: Some unimportant news has surfaced, readable except for one typo.
explanation.walkthrough: The first E of LEGIBLE becomes an I. Gen is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something negligible is so small or unimportant it can be ignored, which is what trivial means.

clue.text: Soil shortage, lacking depth

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so that letter goes

blocks.note: a dearth is a scarcity
D is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: A gardener complains of thin soil, with not enough depth.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is a common word for the soil in which plants grow.

clue.text: Trail tours, catching a source of entertainment

indicators.note: catching something means taking hold of it, so one piece is held inside another
the source is where something starts, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: trips are journeys or tours
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Tour groups on a walking trail stop to take in a show.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside TRIPS, after its second letter, and E follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To traipse is to walk wearily or trail along, a verb synonym for trail.

clue.text: Moon's changing? Granted - feeling sleepy?

indicators.note: something changing alters its form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of the word, apostrophe dropped
something lent has been granted on loan

explanation.surface: Someone notices the moon's phases shift and, admittedly, starts nodding off.
explanation.definitionFit: Somnolent is a formal adjective for drowsy, the state of wanting to sleep.

clue.text: A dull business redirected Irish police

indicators.note: sent the opposite way, so the phrase is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a drag is something tedious

explanation.surface: Irish police find a tedious case has been reassigned elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A DRAG read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garda Síochána is the national police force of Ireland, usually shortened to Garda.

clue.text: Exiled poet? The sod all but returned

indicators.note: all but means nearly everything, so the final letter is dropped
something returned goes back the way it came, so read it backwards

blocks.note: a divot is a chunk of turf, a sod

explanation.surface: A grumble about a banished poet who has nearly come home.
explanation.walkthrough: DIVOT loses its last letter, then reads backwards. The question mark flags the definition as one example of an exiled poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet Ovid was banished by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea, the classic exiled writer.

clue.text: Religious figure with work after major error?

blocks.note: arch- as a prefix means chief or major
bish is old British slang for a blunder
OP, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A cleric commits a serious blunder and must work afterwards to repair it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the work at the end. Bish is dated British schoolboy slang for a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop is a senior bishop, a high-ranking figure in the Church.

clue.text: Famous, mostly preferred, on the rise? In the second rank

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: to elect is to choose or prefer
B-rated means second class

explanation.surface: A celebrity's standing is climbing, but they are still only second-tier.
explanation.walkthrough: ELECT loses its T and then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone celebrated is widely known and praised, which is what famous means.

clue.text: Fine to move, avoiding black stuff

indicators.note: avoiding something means keeping clear of it, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
to budge is to move slightly
B is the abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Something tells you it is fine to shift, steering clear of dark material.
explanation.walkthrough: BUDGE drops its B. 'black stuff' looks like one phrase; split it, and 'stuff' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fudge as nonsense matches stuff in the dismissive sense, as in 'stuff and nonsense'.

clue.text: Confused us with details in tiredness

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone, worn out, has bewildered us with too much fine print.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is a state of physical or mental weariness, a formal word for tiredness.

clue.text: Preliminary to photography for one quark?

blocks.note: say means for example
quark is a soft fresh cheese

explanation.surface: A physicist's subatomic particle seems to be getting ready for a photo shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quark' looks like the physics particle; here it is the soft cheese, and 'for one' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers tell their subjects to say cheese so that they smile before the picture is taken.

clue.text: Extreme to attempt a filibuster, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: furthest or utmost
second meaning, read as two words: talking more than anyone else

explanation.walkthrough: A filibuster is a tactic of speaking at great length to delay a vote, so the speaker tries to speak the most.
explanation.definitionFit: Uttermost is a literary word for most extreme or farthest; split, it is a phrase for talking the most.

clue.text: Find fault with one in competition for building work

blocks.note: to carp is to complain pettily
an entry is one competitor's submission

explanation.surface: A judge criticises one contestant in a construction competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpentry is the craft of making wooden structures, a kind of building work.

clue.text: Insect flying etc around stack of hay

indicators.note: letters flying about are scattered and land in a fresh order
going around something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
a rick is a haystack

explanation.surface: Insects and the like are buzzing round a haystack.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket is a chirping insect related to the grasshopper.

clue.text: Continue to be lecherous, abandoning South English town

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so that letter goes

blocks.note: to lust is to feel lecherous desire
to carry on is to continue
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A man keeps up his leering ways while leaving the south for an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: LUST ON ('continue to be lecherous', in the sense of lust on) loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Luton is a town in Bedfordshire, north of London, known for its airport.

clue.text: Last in exam? Currently woman's first in exam

indicators.note: the first in a word is its opening letter, so only that one is taken

blocks.note: now means at present
her is the possessive for a woman
the opening letter of the second exam

explanation.surface: A student came bottom in one exam and now tops the next.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as a playful paraphrase: finishing last means coming nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To come nowhere in a race or contest is to be unplaced, the idiom for finishing at the bottom.

clue.text: Song that gets mighty Thor dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and land in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tune so catchy that even the powerful Norse god starts to dance.
explanation.definitionFit: I Got Rhythm is a Gershwin standard from the 1930 musical Girl Crazy.

clue.text: Drug featured in musical item the writer's set around university

indicators.note: something set around another encloses it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: op, short for opus, is a numbered musical work
the writer is I, and 'the writer's' as 'the writer is' gives I'M
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A narcotic appears in a stage musical number the author wrote around campus life.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is the setter, so I'M; U goes between its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Opium is a narcotic made from the poppy, the source of morphine and heroin.

clue.text: Unpleasant letters often asterisked among unknown characters

indicators.note: something among others sits in their midst, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: y is an algebraic unknown
the middle letters of a familiar swear word, usually printed as asterisks
the second of the two unknowns, a pair of y characters

explanation.surface: Nasty swear words with starred-out letters are scattered among strangers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unknown characters' is two letter y's, algebra's unknowns; the letters newspapers star out in the F-word sit between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Yucky is informal for disgusting or nasty, a synonym of unpleasant.

clue.text: Increase threatening sound, scaring off Liberal

blocks.note: a growl is a menacing noise

explanation.definitionFit: To grow is to become larger, so it is a plain verb synonym for increase.

clue.text: Sketch second team's colours

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
to milk a situation is to exploit it

explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Klimt was the Austrian painter of The Kiss, a leading Vienna Secession artist.

clue.text: Impudence to steal part of skeleton

blocks.note: cheek is insolence
to bone is old slang for to steal

explanation.surface: Someone has the nerve to pilfer bones from a skeleton.
explanation.walkthrough: Bone meaning to pinch is old slang the solver may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheekbone, or zygomatic bone, is one of the bones of the face and thus of the skeleton.

clue.text: Institute backtracked without thought and without wanting to cause offence

clue.text: Name bird seen in central part of regatta venue

explanation.definitionFit: To entitle a book is to give it a title, that is, to name it.
